summary: Defines a YANG data model for Access Control Lists, ordered sets of rules that match packets and define actions on them, to configure forwarding behavior.

plainLanguage.summary: An access control list is the ordered list of rules a network device uses to decide what to do with each packet. Every manufacturer spells that list differently, so a tool that manages filters has to be taught each one. This document gives the industry one common way of writing the list down, in YANG, and leaves room for each vendor to add its own extras.

questions: what is an access control list
what is the yang acl model
how does an ace match packets
what does the reject action do in an acl
subtitle: A standard YANG schema for writing access control lists: ordered rules that match packets and say what to do with them.

tldr.problem: Every vendor models access control lists differently, so configuring packet filters across devices means learning each vendor's own data model.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8519 defines two YANG 1.1 modules: a generic ACL module and a packet-fields module. An ACL is an ordered list of entries, each pairing match criteria with actions, and the base model can be augmented for extra protocols or vendor features.
tldr.outcome: Vendors get a common base model for ACL configuration that they can extend, and they advertise what they support through feature statements.

facts.label: Headers with matching rules
facts.value: Ethernet, IPv4, IPv6, TCP, UDP, ICMP

today: RFC 8519 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating document, so it remains the registered YANG model for access control list configuration, alongside the packet-fields and ethertypes modules registered with it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
An Access Control List is one of the basic elements used to configure device-forwarding behavior. It is used in many networking technologies such as Policy-Based Routing and firewalls. An ACL is a user-ordered set of rules that is used to filter traffic on a networking device, and each rule is represented by an Access Control Entry.

Each ACE has a group of match criteria and a group of actions. The match criteria allow for the definition of packet headers and metadata, the contents of which must match the definitions. Packet header matches apply to fields visible in the packet such as address, Class of Service, or port number. In case a vendor supports it, metadata matches apply to fields associated with the packet that are not in the packet header, such as the input interface or the length of the packet as received over the wire.

The actions specify what to do with the packet when the matching criteria are met. These actions are any operations that would apply to the packet, such as counting, policing, or simply forwarding. The list of potential actions is unbounded, depending on the capabilities of the networking device.

The matching of filters and actions in an ACE is triggered only after the application, or attachment, of the ACL to an interface, a VRF interface, a vty/tty session, a QoS policy, or routing protocols, amongst various other configuration attachment points. Once attached, it is used for filtering traffic using the match criteria in the ACEs and taking appropriate actions that have been configured against that ACE. In order to apply an ACL to any attachment point other than an interface, vendors would have to augment the ACL YANG model.
sections.plainLanguage: An access control list is a numbered set of rules. Each rule says which packets it applies to, by describing their headers or other facts about them, and what to do with the ones that match. The list only does anything once it is attached to something, such as an interface or a routing protocol, and the first rule that matches decides the fate of the packet.

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.content:
This document defines a YANG 1.1 data model for the configuration of ACLs. The model defines matching rules for commonly used protocols such as Ethernet, IPv4, IPv6, TCP, UDP and ICMP. If more protocols need to be supported in the future, this base model can be augmented, and an example of such an augmentation can be seen in Appendix A.

ACL implementations in every device may vary greatly in terms of the filter constructs and actions that they support. Therefore, this document proposes a model that can be augmented by standard extensions and vendor proprietary models.
sections.plainLanguage: The point is a common base that everybody can build on. The model covers the headers that almost every filter needs, and anything else can be added by augmenting it, either with a standard extension or with a vendor's own module.

sections.title: Understanding ACL Filters and Actions
sections.content:
Although different vendors have different ACL data models, there is a common understanding of what an ACL is. A network system usually has a list of ACLs, and each ACL contains an ordered list of rules, also known as ACEs. Each ACE has a group of match criteria and a group of actions. Packet header matching applies to fields visible in the packet such as address, CoS, or port number, and metadata matching applies to fields associated with the packet that are not in the packet header, such as the input interface, packet length, or source or destination prefix length. The actions can be any sort of operation from logging to rate-limiting or dropping to simply forwarding. Actions on the first matching ACE are applied with no processing of subsequent ACEs.

The model also includes a container to hold overall operational state for each ACL and for each ACE. One ACL can be applied to multiple targets within the device, such as the interface of a networking device, or applications and features running in the device. When applied to interfaces of a networked device, distinct ACLs are defined for the ingress, or input, and egress, or output, interface.

The use of feature statements in the model allows vendors to advertise match rules they are capable and willing to support. There are two sets of feature statements a device needs to advertise. The first set specifies the capability of the device, with features such as being able to match on Ethernet headers or on IPv4 headers. The second set specifies the combinations of headers the device is willing to support, with features such as plain IPv6 ACL supported or Ethernet, IPv4 and IPv6 ACL combinations supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things make the model portable. First, the rule that the first matching entry wins, so the order of the list is the whole meaning. Second, the feature statements, which let a device say in advance what it can match on, so a management tool does not write a rule the device will reject.

sections.title: The Two Modules
sections.content:
There are two YANG modules in the model. The first module, ietf-access-control-list, defines generic ACL aspects that are common to all ACLs regardless of their type or vendor. In effect, the module can be viewed as providing a generic ACL superclass. It imports the second module, ietf-packet-fields. The match container in ietf-access-control-list uses groupings in ietf-packet-fields to specify match fields such as port numbers or protocols. The combination of if-feature checks and must statements allows for the selection of relevant match fields that a user can define rules for.

If there is a need to define a new matches choice, such as IP Flow Information Export, the container matches can be augmented.
sections.plainLanguage: The split is deliberate. One module holds the structure of a list and what it does, and the other holds the packet fields to match on. That way a device that supports one protocol but not another can support one part of the second module, and a new field can be added without touching the first.

sections.title: The Access Control List Module
sections.content:
The ietf-access-control-list module defines the acls container that has a list of each acl. Each acl has information identifying the access list by a name and a list of aces of rules associated with that name. Each of the entries in the list, indexed by the string name, has containers defining matches and actions.

The model defines several ACL types and actions in the form of identities and features. Features are used by implementors to select the ACL types the system can support, and identities are used to validate the types that have been selected. These types are implicitly inherited by the ace, thus safeguarding against misconfiguration of ace types in an acl.

The matches define criteria used to identify patterns in ietf-packet-fields. The choice statements within the match container allow for the selection of one header within each of the l2, l3 or l4 headers. The actions define the behavior to undertake once a match has been identified. In addition to permit and deny actions, a logging option allows for a match to be logged that can later be used to determine which rule was matched upon. The model also defines the ability for ACLs to be attached to a particular interface.

Statistics in the ACL can be collected for an ace or for an interface, and the feature statements defined for statistics can be used to determine whether statistics are being collected per ace or per interface. The three forwarding actions are accept, which accepts the packet, drop, which drops the packet without sending any ICMP error message, and reject, which drops the packet and sends an ICMP error message to the source. The logging actions are log-syslog, which writes the information to the system log, and log-none, which does not log the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The structure is simple: a container of lists, each list a named set of rules, each rule a set of matches and a set of actions. A rule picks at most one header from each of the link, network and transport layers. The actions are a small set of identities that a vendor can extend, and the device can report how many packets and how many bytes each rule matched.

sections.title: Example Configurations
sections.content:
When a lower-port and an upper-port are both present, it represents a range between the lower-port and upper-port, with both the lower-port and upper-port included. When only a port is present, it represents a port, with the operator specifying the range.

The first XML example represents a configuration where TCP traffic from source ports 16384, 16385, 16386 and 16387 is dropped. The ACL is named sample-port-acl and has the type ipv4-acl-type. It holds one ACE named rule1 whose matches container specifies the tcp header and a source-port with a lower-port of 16384 and an upper-port of 16387. Its actions container sets forwarding to drop.

The second XML example represents a configuration where all IPv4 ICMP echo requests are dropped. The ACL is named sample-icmp-acl. Its single rule matches an ipv4 header with protocol 1 and an icmp header with type 8 and code 0, and its actions container sets forwarding to drop.

A third example represents a configuration of a single port, port 21, that accepts TCP traffic, using an ACL named sample-ipv4-acl with the type ipv4-acl-type.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the shape of a rule in XML. One drops TCP traffic coming from a range of source ports, one drops ICMP echo requests, and one accepts TCP traffic on a single port. A range is written with the lowest and highest port, and both ends are included.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The YANG modules specified in this document define a schema for data that is designed to be accessed via network management protocol such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. The lowest NETCONF layer is the secure transport layer, and the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is Secure Shell. The lowest RESTCONF layer is HTTPS, and the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is TLS.

The NETCONF Access Control Model provides the means to restrict access for particular NETCONF or RESTCONF users to a preconfigured subset of all available protocol operations and content.

There are a number of data nodes defined in these YANG modules that are writable, creatable or deletable, and these data nodes may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. Write operations to these data nodes without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations.

The list of access control entries on the device is the first sensitive subtree. Unauthorized write access to this list can allow intruders to modify the entries so as to permit traffic that should not be permitted, or deny traffic that should be permitted. The former may result in a denial of service attack or compromise the device, and the latter may result in a denial of service attack. The impact of an unauthorized read access of the list will allow an attacker to determine which rules are in effect, to better craft an attack.

The logging node of an entry specifies the ability to log packets that match that entry. Unauthorized write access to this node can allow intruders to enable logging on one or many entries, overwhelming the server in the process. Unauthorized read access of this node can allow intruders to access logging information, which could be used to craft an attack on the server.
sections.plainLanguage: Two parts of the configuration are worth protecting. The rules themselves: an attacker who can rewrite them can open the network up or shut it down, and even reading them tells them what the device is enforcing. And the logging settings, because an attacker who can turn logging on everywhere can flood the server with log messages.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
This document registers three URIs in the IETF XML Registry: urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-access-control-list, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-packet-fields and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-ethertypes. The registrant contact is the IESG.

This document also registers three YANG modules in the YANG Module Names registry: ietf-access-control-list, ietf-packet-fields and ietf-ethertypes.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA records the three module names and their namespaces, so that the modules can be referenced unambiguously by other models and by tools.
